issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
Martin Alvarez was 58, a dentist who had spent most of his adult life building a steady practice in a North American suburb, and he had always thought of himself as composed, even in difficult situations. That belief changed after the night police officers forced him onto the pavement outside his office building and treated him with a roughness he had never imagined would be directed at him. He had been leaving late after finishing records when an officer shouted at him to stop, rushed him, and pinned him down hard enough that his ribs and shoulder burned; the sound of boots on asphalt, the barked commands, and the pressure of a knee against his body became the details that later returned most vividly. In the months that followed, Martin came to feel that there was something in him that had made the event happen, as if he had failed some invisible test or carried himself in a way that invited it. He also felt that what happened was deeply unfair and that no one had truly answered for it. Those conclusions kept drawing him back to the night outside the office, and the memory would arrive with the force of evidence, as if replaying it might finally explain what he had done wrong. Each time it surfaced, he left the moment more convinced that the event had marked him as someone damaged and exposed. Those beliefs did not sit still as abstract ideas; when the memory came back, it often did so with the force of an accusation, and he would find himself pulled back into the moment as though the event belonged to someone else's life but had somehow been lodged in his own.

The memory had a strangely detached quality for Martin, as if he were observing another man being thrown to the ground, yet it was never distant for long. After the image broke through, he would catch himself thinking that if it could still seize him so completely, there must be something permanently wrong with him. The memory itself seemed to deliver the verdict. When he recalled it, he sometimes heard the same clipped voices and commands in his head, and his chest and ribs would ache in the same places they had hurt that night. He found these returns so unsettling that he began arranging his days to keep anything from stirring them. He avoided stressors of any kind, turned down social invitations, and stopped allowing himself to feel much of anything, whether good or bad, because strong emotion seemed to open the door to the scene. He was especially careful in public spaces. At restaurants he always chose a seat facing the entrance or with a wall behind him, and in his dental office he became preoccupied with exits, hallways, and who might be coming through the front door. That constant sense of danger kept him mentally close to the assault, as if he had to keep reviewing it in order to stay one step ahead of whatever might happen next. On nights when he felt most on edge, the memory was hardest to keep at bay and would come back vivid and unwelcome. Even on ordinary errands he felt threatened by strangers approaching him, not because they had done anything, but because the memory had taught him how quickly an ordinary encounter could turn. He scanned his surroundings constantly, watching hands, uniforms, movement at the edge of his vision.

That vigilance and avoidance had begun to shape the memory itself. Martin noticed that when he tried to keep the experience away, it often came back more sharply, as if his mind were filling in what he had refused to think about. The more he organized his life around not being surprised, the more the event seemed to break into him at odd moments: while he was sterilizing instruments, while waiting for a patient to settle, while sitting in traffic and seeing a patrol car in the distance. Each return carried the same bodily sting and the same half-audible commands, and each one deepened his conviction that something about him had marked him out for humiliation and danger. He had come to believe not only that his life had been damaged, but that it had been altered beyond repair. On difficult days he felt that the trauma had destroyed the life he had built, and that its injustice was made worse by how little had been done about it. Those conclusions made the memories more charged, and the more charged they became, the more he tried to push them away. The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close; he had spent months trying not to think about it, and that very struggle seemed to leave the scene waiting just beneath the surface, ready to break through when he was already feeling most threatened.

Pushing them away, however, had its own cost. Martin kept himself from anything that might stir feeling, which meant fewer conversations with his partner, less patience with patients, and a narrowing world built around safety and control. He slept poorly, often lying awake listening for sounds outside or waking abruptly after light dozing, already scanning the room. At the office he rearranged his schedule to reduce stress and found himself checking the waiting room and parking lot repeatedly, as if vigilance could prevent another sudden violation. Each time he relied on those precautions to get through the day, he felt another small piece of evidence that he could not manage without them, and that quiet accumulation fed the thought that he was not coping the way he should. The more he organized life around protection, the more certain he became that he was fragile now in a way he had never been before. Yet each effort to stay protected also reinforced the sense that the threat was still present. When a stranger approached him on the sidewalk, his body reacted before his mind could reason it through, and when he noticed how quickly he tensed, the memory of being forced down would intrude again. At that point the old conclusions returned with fresh force: that he had somehow brought it on himself, that nothing had been made right, that his life was no longer the one he had known. The more he lived that way, the more the trauma organized his days, until even ordinary settings felt like places where danger might reappear.

By the time Martin sought help, he was exhausted by the constant scanning, the broken sleep, and the way his practice and relationship had become smaller around his fear. What finally brought him in was the realization that he could no longer sit through a workday without choosing the safest chair, checking every doorway, and bracing whenever anyone unfamiliar stepped into view. He said he did not want to keep living as if the world were about to ambush him again, but he was also afraid that if he let his guard down, the memory would come back with the same voices, the same pain, and the same conviction that his life had been stolen from him for no reason at all.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs and the memory, but it does not clearly state that the negative appraisals cause or drive the traumatic memory to return.

The vignette does not clearly say the memory leads to negative appraisals; the beliefs are described as intensifying with the memories, but a direct memory-to-belief causal link is not established in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows a sense of threat and memory, but it does not explicitly convey that perceived threat drives the traumatic memory to intrude.
The vignette does not clearly indicate that threat causes negative appraisals; it links threat to scanning and fear, but not to the formation of self-blaming beliefs.
The vignette describes avoidance and safety behaviors, but it does not clearly state that these strategies cause the memory to return.

The vignette does not clearly show maladaptive strategies producing negative appraisals; it says the strategies reinforce threat and are followed by beliefs, but not that they directly drive the beliefs.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette shows negative beliefs and the memory, but it does not clearly state that the negative appraisals cause or drive the traumatic memory to return.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly say the memory leads to negative appraisals; the beliefs are described as intensifying with the memories, but a direct memory-to-belief causal link is not established in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows a sense of threat and memory, but it does not explicitly convey that perceived threat drives the traumatic memory to intrude.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly indicate that threat causes negative appraisals; it links threat to scanning and fear, but not to the formation of self-blaming beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes avoidance and safety behaviors, but it does not clearly state that these strategies cause the memory to return.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show maladaptive strategies producing negative appraisals; it says the strategies reinforce threat and are followed by beliefs, but not that they directly drive the beliefs.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
